exercises.prompt:
`P` has a `const` constructor and no `==` override. `Q` is the same but overrides `==` and `hashCode` to compare `x`. What does this line print?

```dart
print('${{P(1), P(1)}.length} ${{Q(1), Q(1)}.length} ${{const P(1), const P(1)}.length}');
```

feedback.message: Close. Two identical `const` expressions are canonicalized into one object, so even identity equality sees them as the same.

hints: What does the compiler do with two identical constant expressions?
exercises.solution: `P(1)` twice (not `const`) creates two objects that are not `==`, so the set has **2**. `Q` compares by value, so its set has **1**. `const P(1)` twice is a single canonical object, so that set also has **1**. (The analyzer even warns that two elements of that set literal are equal.) Output: `2 1 1`.

hints: Mixins are applied left to right on top of the superclass.
The last mixin applied is the closest to the class, so its member wins.
exercises.solution: In `C`, the chain is `Base`, then `A`, then `B`, so `B`'s `hi` overrides the others: `B`. In `D` the order is reversed, so `A` wins. Output: `BA`.

exercises.prompt:
What does this print?

```dart
final list = [3, 1, 2]
  ..sort()
  ..add(0);
print(list);
```

feedback.message: Not yet. The cascades run in order: first sort, then add 0 at the end.

hints: A cascade calls each member on the same object, in order, and the whole expression is that object.
exercises.solution: The list is sorted to `[1, 2, 3]`, then `0` is appended. The cascade expression's value is the list itself, so `list` is `[1, 2, 3, 0]`. (Without cascades, `[3, 1, 2].sort()` would return `void`.)

exercises.prompt: `Shape` is an abstract class with abstract `name` and `area()`, and a concrete method `describe()`. A class declares `class Circle implements Shape`. Which members must `Circle` define itself?

options.label: Only `name` and `area()`
options.feedback: Not yet. That would be enough with `extends`, which inherits `describe()`. `implements` inherits no code.

options.label: `name`, `area()` and `describe()`
options.feedback: Yes. Implementing an interface means providing every member yourself.

options.label: None: an abstract class's interface is optional
options.feedback: Not yet. The compiler reports every missing member of the implemented interface.

options.label: Only `describe()`
options.feedback: Not yet. The abstract members must be implemented in any case.

hints: What is the difference between `extends` and `implements`?
exercises.solution: With `implements`, a class takes on another class's **interface** only, so it must implement all of its members, including `describe()`. With `extends` it would inherit `describe()` and only need the abstract members.

exercises.prompt: An extension adds `String get shout` to `String`. What happens with `dynamic d = 'hey'; print(d.shout);`?

options.label: It prints `HEY!`.
options.feedback: Not yet. Extensions are chosen from the static type, and `dynamic` has no extensions.

options.label: It compiles, and throws a `NoSuchMethodError` at run time.
options.feedback: Yes. `dynamic` turns off checking, so it compiles; at run time `String` has no `shout` member.

options.label: It does not compile.
options.feedback: Not yet. Calls on `dynamic` are never checked at compile time.

options.label: It prints `null`.
options.feedback: Not yet. A missing member is an error, not `null`.

hints: Are extension members part of the object, or resolved by the compiler?
exercises.solution: Extension members are resolved **statically**. The static type of `d` is `dynamic`, so the compiler does not look for extensions, and at run time the `String` object has no member called `shout`: `NoSuchMethodError`. With `final s = 'hey';` (static type `String`), `s.shout` prints `HEY!`.

exercises.prompt: You publish a package with a class `Cache`. Other packages should be able to write their own implementations of its interface, but must not inherit its implementation code. Which modifier fits?

options.label: `interface class Cache`
options.feedback: Yes. Other libraries may implement it but not extend it.

options.label: `base class Cache`
options.feedback: Not yet. `base` is the opposite: it allows extending but forbids implementing.

options.label: `final class Cache`
options.feedback: Not yet. `final` forbids both, so nobody could provide their own implementation.

options.label: `mixin class Cache`
options.feedback: Not yet. That lets others use it as a mixin, inheriting its code.

hints: Look for the modifier named after what others may do with it.
exercises.solution: `interface class Cache` lets other libraries `implement` it while forbidding `extends`, so they can supply their own implementation but never depend on the internal details of yours. Inside your own library, you can still extend it.
